Full Title: A longitudinal study of parent-child relationship and behavioral problems in children aged 3 to 6: the mediating role of screen time
Authors: Xiaojun Ling, Mengqi Li, Jiahui Sun
Journal: Frontiers in Psychology, Section: Media Psychology, Volume 17, 2026
DOI: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1794353
Publication Date: May 25, 2026

Study Design: Longitudinal with three assessment waves spaced 4 months apart.
Sample Size: 532 valid cases (initial recruitment n=619; attrition of 87 participants, 14.1%).
Participant Age: Children aged 3 to 6 years (mean age 3.99 years, SD=0.85). Age breakdown: 198 children age 3 (37.2%), 150 age 4 (28.2%), 184 age 5 (34.6%); 289 boys (54.3%), 243 girls (45.7%).
Country/Population: Fuyang City, Anhui Province, China; data collected via Wenjuanxing platform; all respondents were mothers.
Time Points: Three waves (T1, T2, T3), 4 months apart.

Measurement - Parent-Child Relationship: Child-Parent Relationship Scale (CPRS), Chinese revised version by Deng (2013). Two subscales: Closeness (7 items, alpha=0.882) and Conflict (8 items, alpha=0.895). Five-point Likert scale (1=not at all true to 5=completely true).
Measurement - Screen Time: Two items measuring average daily electronic device use on weekdays and weekends; weighted average = (weekday average x 5 + weekend average x 2)/7.
Measurement - Behavioral Problems: Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Externalizing problems (alpha=0.891) via Hyperactivity/Inattention and Conduct Problems subscales (5 items each). Internalizing problems (alpha=0.853) via Emotional Symptoms and Peer Problems subscales (5 items each). Three-point scale (1=not true to 3=certainly true).

Main Statistical Results:
Conflictual parent-child relationship (T1) -> Internalizing behavioral problems (T3): beta=0.476, p<0.001, 95% CI [0.302, 0.650]
Conflictual parent-child relationship (T1) -> Externalizing behavioral problems (T3): beta=0.273, p<0.05, 95% CI [0.118, 0.428]
Conflictual parent-child relationship (T1) -> Screen time (T2): beta=0.208, p<0.001, 95% CI [0.094, 0.322]
Screen time (T2) -> Internalizing problems (T3): beta=0.148, p<0.05, 95% CI [0.011, 0.285]
Screen time (T2) -> Externalizing problems (T3): beta=0.149, p<0.05, 95% CI [0.016, 0.282]
Indirect effect Conflict -> Screen time -> Internalizing: beta=0.031, p<0.05, 95% CI [-0.026, 0.088]
Indirect effect Conflict -> Screen time -> Externalizing: beta=0.031, p<0.05, 95% CI [-0.022, 0.084]
Close parent-child relationship (T1) -> Screen time (T2): beta=0.006, p>0.05 (not significant), 95% CI [-0.088, 0.100]
Close parent-child relationship (T1) -> Internalizing problems (T3): beta=-0.157, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.294, -0.020]
Close parent-child relationship (T1) -> Externalizing problems (T3): beta=-0.213, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.346, -0.080]
Indirect effects of Close relationship via screen time: not significant for either internalizing or externalizing problems.

Model fit: chi2(7)=19.27, p<0.05; RMSEA=0.057, 90% CI [0.028, 0.089]; CFI=0.950; TLI=0.917; SRMR=0.028.

Stated Limitations (verbatim from authors):
- The present study did not include baseline levels of key variables, which may have resulted in insufficient control for stable between-person differences at initial assessment. As a consequence, some of the observed indirect effects may partially reflect pre-existing levels of the constructs rather than purely developmental processes.
- The screen time measure does not capture important contextual information that may be critical for understanding its role in child development.
- All core variables in the present study were reported by a single informant; reliance on a single source of information remains a methodological limitation.
- The study captures only a limited developmental time window. The relatively short measurement interval may not adequately reflect the dynamic interplay among screen time, parent-child relationships, and behavioral problems over time. Accordingly, the generalizability of the findings across longer developmental periods should be interpreted with caution.
- The association between parent-child relationships and children behavioral outcomes does not necessarily operate directly through screen time; underlying mechanisms are likely more complex, potentially involving indirect pathways through other mediating or moderating processes.
- Although participants were recruited through kindergartens and classes, the present study did not explicitly model the nested data structure (e.g., children within classes or schools). Thus, potential clustering effects cannot be entirely ruled out.
- Caution is warranted when interpreting the causal implications of the observed mediating effects.
